SuperGrasp: Single-View Object Grasping via Superquadric
Similarity Matching, Evaluation, and Refinement
Lijingze Xiao†, Jinhong Du†, Yang Cong∗, Supeng Diao, Yu Ren
Abstract—Robotic grasping from single-view observations re-
mains a critical challenge in manipulation. Existing methods
still struggle to generate stable and valid grasp poses when
confronted with incomplete geometric information. To address
these limitations, we propose SuperGrasp, a novel two-stage
framework for single-view grasping with parallel-jaw grippers
that decomposes the grasping process into initial grasp pose
generation and subsequent grasp evaluation and refinement.
In the first stage, we introduce a Similarity Matching Module
that efficiently retrieves grasp candidates by matching the input
single-view point cloud with a pre-computed primitive dataset
based on superquadric coefficients. In the second stage, we
propose E-RNet, an end-to-end network that expands the grasp-
aware region and takes the initial grasp closure region as a local
anchor region, enabling more accurate and reliable evaluation
and refinement of grasp candidates. To enhance generalization,
we construct a primitive dataset containing 1.5k primitives for
similarity matching and collect a large-scale point cloud dataset
with 100k stable grasp labels from 124 objects for network
training. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-
world environments demonstrate that our method achieves stable
grasping performance and strong generalization across varying
scenes and novel objects.
Index Terms—single-view grasping, superquadric similarity
matching, grasp evaluation and refinement.
I. INTRODUCTION
Grasping is a fundamental capability in robotic manipu-
lation and has shown great potential in household service
and industrial production-line applications in structured en-
vironments. However, grasping objects in unstructured envi-
ronments remains challenging, especially under single-view
observations, due to incomplete and noisy visual inputs.
Effectively exploiting such degraded geometric information
to generate stable grasp poses is still difficult for existing
methods.
Superquadrics [1] were introduced into computer vision
in the late twentieth century as a compact representation of
geometric primitives. Later, with improvements to fitting algo-
rithms by [2], [3], superquadrics became increasingly effective
for representing object geometry directly from point clouds.
This progress has inspired new solutions for robotic grasping.
For example, Wu et al. [4] take point clouds as input, compute
multiple graspable regions based on superquadric coefficients,
and then sample grasp poses accordingly, achieving promising
results. However, these methods are generally developed under
the assumption of complete point clouds. For single-view point
clouds, geometric representation still suffers from substantial
difficulties in both shape and scale alignment.

With the rapid development of neural networks, data-
driven grasping methods, including sampling-and-evaluation
pipelines [5]–[7] and end-to-end approaches [7]–[13], have
achieved significant progress in this field. Representative meth-
ods such as GPD [5] and PointNetGPD [6] adopt a two-
stage framework. They first sample grasp candidates from
point-cloud geometry and then classify these candidates using
neural networks. However, due to geometric incompleteness
in sparse point clouds, the sampled grasp candidates are
often unreliable, and the subsequent evaluation models may
lack robustness. To address this issue, end-to-end methods
[9]–[12], [14]–[16] directly predict grasp poses from input
point clouds. Although effective, these methods usually require
large-scale training data to learn feasible grasp poses, and their
generalization to unseen objects is still limited.
Inspired by chen et al. [17], we propose SuperGrasp, a novel
two-stage grasping pipeline, to address the above challenges
through a similarity-matching module and a more robust eval-
uation and refinement module. Specifically, in the first stage,
we estimate superquadric coefficients from the target object
point cloud under a single-view observation to represent its
geometric shape. We then perform similarity matching against
a primitive database constructed offline using superquadric
coefficients, where both shape and scale are considered. The
grasp poses of the top-Nmost similar primitive objects are
subsequently transformed to the target object point cloud,
yielding rich and effective grasp candidates.arXiv:2603.29254v1  [cs.RO]  31 Mar 2026

In the second stage, to enable more reliable evaluation and
refinement, we design a new evaluation-refinement network
based on PointNet++ [18] as the backbone. The network
enlarges the grasp-aware region and takes the initial grasp
closure local region as an anchor region. Based on this design,
it jointly analyzes the geometric features within the initial
grasp closure region and the surrounding spatial geometric
context, thereby enabling more accurate and robust prediction
of grasp feasibility as well as refinement feasibility.
To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we
conduct extensive grasping experiments in both simulation and
real-world environments across multiple scenarios. The exper-
imental results demonstrate that our method achieves strong
stability while maintaining excellent generalization capability.
The task pipeline is shown in Fig. 1. Our main contributions
are summarized as follows:
•We propose a superquadric-based similarity matching
method. It represents a target object with incomplete
point clouds using multiple primitive objects with similar
shapes and scales from a complete point cloud database
and transfers high-quality grasp candidates from the
matched primitives to the target object, thereby providing
rich and effective grasp candidates.
•We propose a new evaluation-refinement network that
expands the grasp-aware region and takes the initial grasp
closure local region as an anchor region. This design
enables the network to analyze not only the geometric
features within the grasp closure region but also the geo-
metric relationships of the surrounding points, leading to
more robust prediction of grasp feasibility and refinement
feasibility.
•We conduct extensive experiments in both simulation and
real-world settings to verify the effectiveness of the pro-
posed method. In particular, all training data are generated
in simulation and the model is directly transferred to real-
world scenes without any real-world fine-tuning.
The code and data associated with this work will be made
publicly available.
II. RELATEDWORK
Grasping has long been a focus of robotics research. With
the rapid development of computer vision and neural networks,
grasping methods have become increasingly diverse. In this
section, we introduce superquadrics and discuss two primary
research directions in robotic grasping.
A. Superquadrics
Superquadrics [1]–[3] provide a unified representation for
regular geometric primitives such as cubes, cylinders, spheres,
and ellipsoids using only a small number of parameters. A
superquadric can be implicitly represented as

Superquadrics are widely applied in object modeling, shape
approximation, and scene understanding due to their low-
dimensional representation and strong geometric interpretabil-
ity. They are particularly effective for modeling objects with
nearly convex structures, and the recovered parameters can
directly convey the graphical, orientational, and shape charac-
teristics of the objects.
B. Two-Stage Grasping
Two-stage grasping methods typically decompose the prob-
lem into grasp candidate generation and grasp evaluation. GPD
[5] first samples grasp candidates in 3D space, labels them
using force closure analysis [19], and trains a CNN to predict
grasp feasibility from grasp-aligned projections. PointNetGPD
[6] further improves this paradigm by directly encoding the
point cloud within the grasp region using a PointNet-based
architecture for grasp quality prediction. Later, 3DSGrasp
[20] introduced 3D reconstruction to compensate for missing
geometric information in point clouds, thus improving both
the generation of grasp candidates and the accuracy of grasp
feasibility analysis. However, due to the continuous and high-
dimensional nature of the grasp space, exhaustive spatial
sampling is inherently time-consuming and inefficient.
To address this issue, Chen et al. [17] proposed to generate
grasp candidates through multi-Level similarity matching. By
measuring the geometric and semantic similarity between the
target object and objects stored in a database, grasp poses from
the most similar objects can be transferred to the target object.
Nevertheless, under incomplete geometric observations, the
matching quality of such methods often degrades significantly.

C. End-to-End Grasping
To address sampling inefficiency, Fang et al. [10] proposed
an end-to-end network frameworks that decouple and dis-
cretize grasp representations. These models take point clouds
as input and directly output grasp candidates with quality
scores, relying on large-scale training data to ensure strong
generalization. Methods [11], [12] further introduced grasp
refinement strategies, first analyzing global point cloud in-
formation to obtain coarse grasp poses, then refining them
using local geometric details, fully leveraging point cloud
spatial information and improving grasp success rates. Meth-
ods [21], [22] proposed V AE-based models that encodes point
clouds into implicit features and decodes them to generate
6-DoF grasp poses. However, the aforementioned methods
still exhibit limited generalization capabilities when handling
variations in scene and object shapes.
III. PROBLEMFORMULATION
We formulate the task as tabletop decluttering with a
robotic arm equipped with a parallel-jaw gripper, although
the proposed framework can also be applied to target-object
grasping. Notably, only a single fixed depth camera is deployed
within a50 cm×50 cmworkspace to capture the scene point
cloud. The model takes as input the target object point cloud
together with the global scene point cloudX∈RN×3, and
outputs a grasp poseg, defined as:
g={p, R, w},

senting the gripper orientation,p= (x, y, z)∈R3×1denotes
the gripper position, andw∈Rdenotes the gripper width.
Our framework generates an initial set of grasp candidates
G={g 1, g2, . . .}and then selects the final graspg bestthrough

IV. METHOD
A. Overview
Single-view grasping remains challenging due to missing
geometric information and sensor noise. To improve the ef-
ficiency and reliability of grasping, we propose SuperGrasp,
a new two-stage framework. First, we introduce a geometric
similarity matching strategy to generate grasp candidates(see
Sec. IV-B). Second, we propose an end-to-end evaluation and
refinement network, termed E-RNet, to evaluate the stability
of the grasp and refine it locally(see Sec. IV-D).
B. Superquadric Similarity Matching
Superquadrics can represent a complete object shape us-
ing only six parameters{a x, ay, az, ϵ1, ϵ2,g}, providing an
alternative grasping paradigm. However, in the single-view
setting, point clouds are often unclosed, making it difficult
to accurately estimate superquadric coefficients. This leads to
biases in both shape and scale, resulting in unstable grasp
candidate quality and insufficient coverage. To address this
issue, we propose a superquadric-based similarity matching
method, as illustrated in Fig.4.

C. Data Collection
We select 124 graspable objects with various shapes and
sizes from YCB [23], KIT [24], and DexNet [25] to construct
the object dataset. We then build a workspace equipped witha single depth camera in the PyBullet [26] simulation envi-
ronment. For each scene, five objects are randomly dropped
into the workspace, and one of them is randomly designated
as the target object. The target object point cloud is obtained
from the object mask, and rich grasp candidates are generated
using the strategy described in Sec. IV-B. Finally, one grasp
pose is randomly sampled for execution.
For label assignment, unlike methods [5], [6], which grade
grasp poses based on analytic metrics, we directly determine
the label according to the execution outcome in simulation.
Specifically, during execution, if the gripper collides with
surrounding objects, the label is directly set to 0. If the gripper
successfully lifts the target object, then reorients it to a pose
with the gripper approach axis aligned vertically downward,
and the grasp remains stable under a downward disturbance
force of1 Napplied for0.5 s, as shown in Fig. 5, the label is
set to 1. All other cases are labeled as 0.
Although the grasp candidates have already been coarsely
filtered, slight deviations may still lead to grasp failure in
dense cluttered scenes. To exploit the reproducibility of the
simulation environment, we further fine-tune the initial grasp
pose during data collection. Specifically, we first deepen the
grasp by translating it0.008 malong the approach direction ,
and then additionally rotate it around the approach direction
by[−15◦,0◦,15◦], resulting in three additional grasp attempts,
as shown in Fig. 5. The refinement labels are defined using
the same criterion as that of the initial grasp. Following the
above strategy, we collect 100K labeled training samples.
D. E-RNet: Evaluation and Refinement Network
In practical grasp execution, due to the angular deviation
between the gripper fingers and the local surface normals
of the object, a certain degree of relative motion may occur
between the gripper and the object during closure. Therefore,
it is insufficient to consider only the grasp closing region; the

in which case slight pose adjustment can play a critical role.
To address these issues, we propose a novel evaluation and
refinement network, termedE-RNet. The overall architecture
is illustrated in Fig. 4.
To enrich grasp-aware perception, we enlarge the initial
gripper closing region. Specifically, the initial grasp pose is
first deepened by0.008 malong the approach direction, and
then additionally rotated around the approach axis by+15◦
and−15◦. For stable learning, we transform the global point
cloud into the gripper coordinate frame and use the enlarged
closing region to crop the local region of interest from the
global point cloud, yielding a cropped point cloud of size
N×3. The cropped point cloud is then fed into a PointNet++
backbone to extract point-wise features of sizeN×128.
To model the relationship between the initial grasp region
and its surrounding space, we further crop the features corre-
sponding to the original grasp closing region, and use a shared
MLP to map the point features into a higher-dimensional
feature space before aggregating them by max pooling into
a1×256feature vector. We treat this pooled feature as the
grasp anchor feature, which encodes not only the geometric
characteristics of the local closing region but also its spatial
relationship with surrounding points. The grasp anchor feature
is then fed into an evaluation classification head implemented
as a three-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) to predict grasp
feasibility. The training loss for this branch is defined as the
cross-entropy loss:

Unlike methods that fine-tune all grasp candidates in a
multi-dimensional pose space to further expand the candidate

anchor and explore the grasp feasibility of its neighboring
regions, which is more efficient and time-saving. Moreover,
unlike Regnet [11], which regresses each candidate towards

grasp. This design provides more refinement flexibility during
inference.
Specifically, the grasp anchor feature is simultaneously fed
into a refinement head implemented as another three-layer
MLP. This branch analyzes the geometric relationships in the
surrounding space and predicts the refinement feasibility of the
initial grasp pose under three candidate adjustments, namely

and rotating it around the approach axis by−15◦,0◦and15◦,
respectively. This branch is trained using the binary cross-

E. Training and Inference Details
During training, we first add random Gaussian noise to
the global point cloud. We then crop the point cloud within
the expanded grasp region and downsample it to 960 points.
Subsequently, the points within the gripper closing region are
further downsampled to 345 points, and their indices in the
expanded grasp-region point cloud are recorded for subsequent
feature cropping. The network is trained in an end-to-end
manner by minimizing the following loss:
L=λ 1Le+λ2Lr.(12)
whereλ 1=λ 2= 1. The network is trained on an NVIDIA
GeForce RTX 4090 GPU for 100 epochs, with a batch size of
128. We use the Adam [28] optimizer with an initial learning
rate of0.001and a weight decay of3×10−4.
During inference, a grasp is executed directly only when
its evaluation score exceeds 0.7. If the maximum evaluation
score is lower than 0.7 but the maximum refinement score
is higher than 0.7, the corresponding initial grasp is further
refined before execution.
V. EXPERIMENTS
We conduct extensive comparative experiments in both sim-
ulation and real-world environments to demonstrate that: 1) the
proposed superquadric similarity matching module can stably
generate rich and effective grasp candidates; 2) the proposed
evaluation and refinement module can accurately evaluate and
refine grasp poses; and 3) the overall framework exhibits
strong generalization capability and real-time performance.
We choose PointNetGPD [6] and Contact-GraspNet [9] as
baselines. For a fair comparison among different methods, we
adopt the following evaluation metrics:
•Grasp Success Rate (GSR):the number of successful
grasps divided by the total number of grasp attempts over
Nscene trials.

A. Simulation Experiments
We construct a50 cm×50 cmgrasping workspace in the
PyBullet [26] simulation environment and deploy a fixed depth
camera to capture scene point clouds. To thoroughly evaluate
the performance of the proposed method, we design three
experimental settings: 1) scenes containing 10 objects (mod-
erately cluttered), 2) scenes containing 20 objects (densely
cluttered), and 3) scenes containing 10 unseen objects, as
illustrated in Fig. 6. For a fair comparison, the same random
seeds are used for all methods in each setting to ensure
identical scene configurations. Each setting is tested over 30
trials. The averaged results are reported in Table I.
As shown in Table I, in the relatively cluttered scene
with 10 objects, our method achieves both an average grasp
success rate and an average task success rate of over95%,
demonstrating its strong stability and efficiency. Compared
with the structurally similar two-stage method PointNetGPD,
our method improves the average grasp success rate by16.32%
and the average task success rate by64.59%. Compared
with the end-to-end Contact-GraspNet baseline, our method
improves the average grasp success rate by16.83%and the
average task success rate by14.67%. These results jointly
validate the superiority of the proposed two-stage framework.
In the more challenging setting with 20 objects, our method
still maintains both the average grasp success rate and the
average task success rate above92%. Specifically, it surpasses
PointNetGPD by33.39%and Contact-GraspNet by17.40%in
grasp success rate, while improving the task success rate by
58.00%and9.84%, respectively. These results demonstrate
the robustness and generalization capability of our method
in highly cluttered environments. When evaluated on unseen
objects that are not included in the training set, our method
still achieves an average task success rate above94%. It
outperforms PointNetGPD by87.63%and Contact-GraspNet
by25%in task success rate, while the average grasp success
rate is improved by55.13%and25.12%, respectively. These

B. Ablation Study
To more precisely analyze the effectiveness of the proposed
framework, we design three ablation settings: 1)Ours (Stage-
1) + PointNetGPD, where our grasp candidate generation
module is combined with the grasp evaluation module of
PointNetGPD to verify the stability and diversity of our
sampling strategy; 2)PointNetGPD + Ours (Stage-2), where
the grasp candidate generation module of PointNetGPD is
combined with our evaluation and refinement module to vali-
date the accuracy and generalization capability of our second
stage; and 3)without the refinement branch, to demonstrate
the necessity of the refinement network and quantify its
contribution during grasp execution.
We conduct the ablation experiments in the same PyBullet
simulation environment under three settings: 1) scenes with
10 objects, 2) scenes with 20 objects, and 3) scenes with 10
unseen objects. Each setting is tested over 30 trials, and the
averaged results are reported in Table I. When our Stage-
1 grasp candidate generation module is combined with the
downstream grasp evaluation module of PointNetGPD, the
task success rate is significantly improved compared with
PointNetGPD in all settings. Specifically, the average task
success rate is improved by43.89%in the 10-object setting,
13.16%in the 20-object setting, and32.77%in the unseen-
object setting. These results confirm that our sampling strategy
can stably provide rich and effective grasp candidates, thereby
improving the overall task success rate. However, the average
grasp success rate decreases in all settings. We attribute this to

the increased number of grasp attempts together with the lim-
ited accuracy of the PointNetGPD evaluation module. Notably,
when the grasp candidate generation module of PointNetGPD
is combined with our Stage-2 module, i.e., grasp evaluation
and refinement, the average grasp success rate is substantially
improved in all three settings. In particular, in the unseen-

Overall, the average task success rate is improved by21.56%.
These results strongly validate the accuracy, robustness, and
generalization capability of our evaluation and refinement
module. In addition, we observe that the refinement branch
has only a limited effect on grasp success rate in the 10-object
setting, but brings clear improvements in the more cluttered
20-object setting and in the unseen-object setting with more
complex surface geometry. Moreover, the average task success
rate across the three settings is further improved by8.39%,
which verifies the necessity and effectiveness of the proposed
refinement strategy.
C. Real-World Experiments
To further validate the strong generalizability of the pro-
posed method, we construct a real-world grasping test set
consisting of 30similarobjects and 25novelobjects whose
shapes and sizes are substantially different from those in the
training set. We design two cluttered real-world scenarios for
evaluation: 1) randomly placing 10 similar objects and 2)
randomly placing 10 novel objects. Each scenario is tested
over 10 trials, and some representative scenarios are shown
in Fig. 7. The hardware setup is as follows. We use a xMate
ER7Pro robotic arm, an AG-105-145 gripper, and a ZED 2i
camera. The entire system is integrated through ROS, and
inverse kinematics is solved using MoveIt! [29]. We employ
FoundationStereo [30] to estimate depth from stereo RGB
images and reconstruct the scene point cloud. We then use
SAM [31] to segment the target object and obtain its point
cloud. The experimental results are reported in Table II.TABLE II

As shown in Table II, in thesimilar-objectsetting, our
method achieves both a grasp success rate and a task success
rate of98%. Specifically, the average grasp success rate ex-
ceeds that of PointNetGPD by39.18%and Contact-GraspNet
by19.05%, while the average task success rate is higher than
that of PointNetGPD by78%and that of Contact-GraspNet by
38%. In the unseen-object setting, our method still maintains
strong performance, with both the grasp success rate and the
task success rate remaining above94%. In this setting, the
average grasp success rate exceeds PointNetGPD by41.74%
and Contact-GraspNet by19.47%, while the average task suc-
cess rate is higher than that of PointNetGPD by85%and that
of Contact-GraspNet by43%. These results demonstrate the
stability and strong generalization capability of the proposed
method. During the experiments, we also record the average
time cost of each stage, as reported in Table III. The time
consumption of each stage in our method is lower than that
of PointNetGPD, especially in the grasp candidate generation
stage, although the overall runtime is slightly higher than that
of Contact-GraspNet.

In addition, we observe that the primary cause of grasp
failure in real-world experiments is self-occlusion of the target
object or occlusion caused by surrounding objects, which
introduces unknown space in the scene and eventually causes
collisions between the gripper and the object during execution.
VI. CONCLUSION
We propose SuperGrasp, a novel two-stage grasping frame-
work which addresses the challenge of grasp sampling un-
der incomplete geometric information through superquadric
representation and similarity matching in the first stage. In
the second stage, we expand the grasp perception range and
utilize the initial gripper closure region as an anchor region
to evaluate and refine grasp candidates. Extensive experi-
ments demonstrate the effectiveness of each stage, and the
overall framework achieves strong performance with robust
generalization across diverse scenarios. Although the real-
time performance of each stage of the grasping process is
better than that of the two-stage PointNetGPD method, the
cumulative time consumption of each stage is slightly higher
than that of the end-to-end method Contact-GraspNet. In
the future, we will continue to study how to improve the
real-time performance of grasping while maintaining strong
generalization and stability.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This document introduces SuperGrasp, a novel two-stage framework for robotic grasping from single-view observations using parallel-jaw grippers. The framework addresses the challenge of generating stable and valid grasp poses with incomplete geometric information.

The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Statement:** Existing single-view grasping methods struggle with incomplete geometric data, leading to unstable and invalid grasp poses.
*   **SuperGrasp Framework:** A two-stage approach comprising:
    *   **Initial Grasp Pose Generation (Similarity Matching Module):** This stage efficiently retrieves grasp candidates by matching the input single-view point cloud with a pre-computed primitive dataset. The matching is based on superquadric coefficients, which represent geometric shapes.
    *   **Grasp Evaluation and Refinement (E-RNet):** This end-to-end network expands the grasp-aware region and uses the initial grasp closure region as an anchor. It analyzes geometric features within and around the closure region for more accurate and reliable evaluation and refinement of grasp candidates.
*   **Dataset Construction:** To enhance generalization, the authors created a primitive dataset with 1.5k primitives for similarity matching and a large-scale point cloud dataset with 100k stable grasp labels from 124 objects for network training.
*   **Contributions:**
    *   A superquadric-based similarity matching method for generating rich and effective grasp candidates by transferring poses from similar primitives.
    *   A novel evaluation-refinement network that considers both the grasp closure region and surrounding geometric context for robust grasp prediction.
    *   Extensive experimental validation in simulation and real-world environments, demonstrating strong stability and generalization, even with models trained solely in simulation.
*   **Background:** The document also provides background on superquadrics as a compact representation of geometric primitives and discusses existing two-stage grasping methods, highlighting their limitations with incomplete data.

nodes.summary: The document describes a two-stage framework called SuperGrasp for robotic grasping. The first stage involves a superquadric-based similarity matching method to generate initial grasp candidates. This method represents target objects with incomplete point clouds using primitive objects from a database and transfers grasp candidates from matched primitives. The second stage utilizes a new evaluation-refinement network, E-RNet, built on PointNet++ to analyze geometric features within the grasp closure region and its surrounding context for more accurate and robust grasp feasibility prediction and refinement. The problem is formulated as tabletop decluttering with a robotic arm and a parallel-jaw gripper, using a single fixed depth camera to capture scene point clouds. The output is a grasp pose defined by position, rotation matrix, and gripper width.

structure.title: METHOD
structure.summary: This partial document discusses advancements in end-to-end grasping for robotic arms, focusing on improving efficiency and generalization. It highlights previous methods that use point clouds to directly output grasp candidates and those that refine grasps using global and local geometric information. The document then formulates the problem of tabletop decluttering and target-object grasping, defining a grasp pose by position, rotation, and width. A new two-stage framework called SuperGrasp is introduced. The first stage, "Superquadric Similarity Matching," aims to generate grasp candidates by representing objects using superquadrics and matching them to a database of primitive objects. This involves precomputing superquadric coefficients for database objects and fitting them to the target object's point cloud. The matching process uses shape parameters and scale ratios to filter candidates.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: The document discusses advancements in robotic grasping, specifically focusing on end-to-end grasping frameworks that take point clouds as input and directly output grasp candidates. It highlights previous methods that use grasp refinement strategies and VAE-based models but notes their limitations in generalization. The document then formulates the problem as tabletop decluttering and introduces a new two-stage framework called SuperGrasp. The first stage, Superquadric Similarity Matching, uses a database of primitive objects to generate initial grasp candidates by matching superquadric representations of the target object. This stage includes pre-computation of superquadric coefficients, fast matching using EMS, and coarse filtering to remove unreasonable candidates. The second stage involves an end-to-end evaluation and refinement network (E-RNet) to assess grasp stability and refine poses. The document also details data collection methods, including object selection, simulation environment setup, and label assignment based on execution outcomes, and describes a refinement process for generating additional training samples.

nodes.title: Stage 1: Grasp Candidate Generation
nodes.summary: The document describes a two-stage framework for grasp pose generation. The first stage involves estimating superquadric coefficients of a target object, comparing them to a database of objects to find similar ones, and transferring their grasp poses. This is followed by a coarse filtering step to remove noisy candidates. The second stage utilizes a PointNet++ network to extract features from an enlarged perception region around initial grasps. These features are then aggregated to form a "grasp anchor feature," which is fed into an evaluation network for grasp feasibility and a refinement network for refinement feasibility. The document also details the data collection process, including object selection, simulation environment setup, and label assignment based on execution outcomes. It further elaborates on the Evaluation and Refinement Network (E-RNet), explaining how it processes local and surrounding spatial information for grasp evaluation and refinement. Finally, it outlines training and inference details, including loss functions, training parameters, and decision-making criteria for grasp execution and refinement. The experimental section mentions comparative experiments and evaluation metrics like Grasp Success Rate (GSR).

nodes.title: Stage 2: Grasp Evaluation and Refinement
nodes.summary:
The partial document describes a novel evaluation and refinement network, termed E-RNet, for grasp pose prediction. The main points covered are:

*   **Gripper Configuration and Refinement Strategy:** Figure 5 illustrates the gripper coordinate system, width, fingertip length, and applied disturbance force. It also details a refinement strategy involving initial downward extension and rotation of the gripper.
*   **Importance of Spatial Information and Pose Adjustment:** The document emphasizes that spatial information around the grasp region is crucial for reliable grasp evaluation. It also highlights the role of slight pose adjustments when initial grasp candidates fail due to clutter or geometric incompleteness.
*   **E-RNet Architecture and Functionality:** E-RNet is proposed to address these issues. It involves an evaluation branch to predict grasp feasibility and a refinement branch to explore neighboring grasp poses.
*   **Enriching Grasp-Aware Perception:** The initial grasp pose is modified by deepening and rotating it to create an enlarged closing region. This local region of interest is cropped from the global point cloud and processed by a PointNet++ backbone.
*   **Grasp Anchor Feature:** Features corresponding to the original grasp closing region are extracted and mapped to a higher-dimensional space before aggregation. This "grasp anchor feature" encodes both local geometric characteristics and spatial relationships with surrounding points.
*   **Grasp Feasibility Evaluation:** The grasp anchor feature is fed into an evaluation classification head (an MLP) to predict grasp feasibility using a cross-entropy loss.
*   **Efficient Refinement Strategy:** Instead of fine-tuning all candidates in a multi-dimensional pose space, E-RNet uses the initial grasp region as a spatial anchor to explore neighboring regions, which is presented as more efficient.
*   **Refinement Head:** The grasp anchor feature is also fed into a refinement head (another MLP) to predict the feasibility of three candidate adjustments: deepening the grasp and rotating it by -15°, 0°, and 15°. This branch uses a binary cross-entropy loss.
*   **Inference Process:** During inference, a grasp is executed if its evaluation score exceeds 0.7. If not, but a refinement score is higher than 0.7, the grasp is refined before execution.
*   **Training Details:** The network is trained end-to-end by minimizing a combined loss of evaluation and refinement losses. Specific training parameters, hardware, and optimizer details are provided.
*   **Experimental Setup:** The document outlines experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed superquadric similarity matching module and the evaluation/refinement module, as well as the overall framework's generalization and real-time performance. Baseline methods and evaluation metrics like Grasp Success Rate (GSR) are mentioned.

structure.title: EXPERIMENTS

*   **E-RNet Architecture and Functionality:**
    *   **Enriching Grasp-Aware Perception:** The initial grasp pose is modified (deepened and rotated) to create an enlarged closing region.
    *   **Local Region of Interest Extraction:** The global point cloud is transformed into the gripper coordinate frame, and the enlarged closing region is used to crop a local point cloud.
    *   **Feature Extraction:** A PointNet++ backbone extracts point-wise features from the cropped point cloud.
    *   **Grasp Anchor Feature:** Features corresponding to the original grasp closing region are further processed and aggregated to create a grasp anchor feature, which encodes local geometry and spatial relationships.
    *   **Evaluation Branch:** The grasp anchor feature is fed into an MLP to predict grasp feasibility using cross-entropy loss.
    *   **Refinement Branch:** The grasp anchor feature is also fed into another MLP to predict the refinement feasibility of the initial grasp pose under three candidate adjustments (deepening and rotating). This branch uses binary cross-entropy loss.
*   **Training and Inference:**
    *   **End-to-End Training:** The network is trained end-to-end by minimizing a combined loss of evaluation and refinement branches.
    *   **Inference Strategy:** A grasp is executed directly if its evaluation score exceeds 0.7. If not, but the maximum refinement score is above 0.7, the grasp is refined before execution.

nodes.title: Real-World Experiments
nodes.summary: This partial document describes real-world experiments evaluating a two-stage grasping framework, "SuperGrasp." The experiments involve two scenarios: objects similar to the training set and objects significantly different in shape and size. The results demonstrate that combining the proposed "Stage-2 module" (grasp evaluation and refinement) with the grasp candidate generation module of PointNetGPD substantially improves grasp success rates, particularly for unseen objects. The document highlights the accuracy, robustness, and generalization capabilities of the proposed evaluation and refinement module. It also details the hardware setup used for the real-world tests, including a robotic arm, gripper, and camera, integrated via ROS. Comparative results against PointNetGPD and Contact-GraspNet are presented in tables, showing superior grasp and task success rates for the proposed method, especially in the unseen-object setting. The time cost of the grasping process is also analyzed, indicating that while the proposed method's cumulative time is slightly higher than Contact-GraspNet, it is significantly faster than PointNetGPD. The document identifies self-occlusion and occlusion by surrounding objects as primary causes of grasp failure in real-world scenarios. Finally, the conclusion reiterates the effectiveness of the SuperGrasp framework, its two stages, and its strong generalization, while acknowledging the need for future improvements in real-time performance.

structure.title: CONCLUSION
structure.summary: This partial document describes a novel two-stage grasping framework called SuperGrasp. The framework addresses challenges in grasp sampling with incomplete geometric information by using superquadric representation and similarity matching in the first stage. The second stage expands grasp perception and refines grasp candidates. The document highlights that self-occlusion and surrounding object occlusion are primary causes of grasp failure in real-world experiments. While SuperGrasp shows effectiveness and generalization, its cumulative time consumption is slightly higher than end-to-end methods, and future work aims to improve real-time performance. The document also includes a comprehensive list of references related to grasping, superquadrics, and computer vision.
